cards.title: Moore's law: the forecast that built tech
cards.body:
In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, noticed that the number of components on a chip was doubling about every year. In 1975 he revised that to roughly every two years. It was an observation, not a law of physics, but the industry treated it as a target and hit it for decades.

The compounding was staggering. Intel's first microprocessor, the 4004 from 1971, had about 2,300 transistors. Today's biggest chips pack tens of billions. Each doubling made computers cheaper, smaller and more powerful, enabling PCs, smartphones and now AI.

Since the mid-2000s the free lunch has shrunk. Individual processor cores stopped getting much faster, so designers added more cores and specialized chips like GPUs. Shrinking transistors further keeps getting harder and more expensive, which is why leading-edge chip-making is now concentrated in a handful of companies.
cards.example: Doubling every two years for 50 years is 25 doublings, a factor of about 33 million. Applied to the 4004's 2,300 transistors from 1971, that gives roughly 77 billion by 2021, the same order of magnitude as the largest chips of the early 2020s.
cards.takeaway: Moore's law was a self-fulfilling forecast: steady doubling, compounded for decades.

cards.title: Hill repeats: speed work in disguise
cards.body:
Hills force you to drive your knees, push off powerfully and use your arms, which builds the strength and power that make you faster on the flat. Because you're moving more slowly uphill, the pounding on your legs is lower than in fast track intervals, so hill repeats are a relatively gentle way to start doing quality work.

The classic session is short and hard. Find a moderate hill that takes 60 to 90 seconds to climb. Run up at a strong effort, about your 5K race effort, keeping tall posture and quick steps. Jog or walk back down as recovery, then repeat.

Keep the effort controlled rather than all-out, and stop the session while your form still looks good. Do hills once a week for a few weeks before adding other fast work.
cards.example: This week: 10 minutes of easy jogging, then 6 × 75 seconds uphill at hard effort, walking or jogging down for recovery, then 10 minutes easy. Next week, add one or two repeats if the last one felt as strong as the first.
cards.takeaway: Hills build speed with less pounding: short, strong, controlled.

cards.title: Negative space: the hidden arrow in FedEx
cards.body:
Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of a design. Beginners treat it as leftover; good designers treat it as a shape in its own right.

The most famous example is the FedEx logo, designed by Lindon Leader in 1994. Between the capital E and the lowercase x sits a white arrow pointing forward, suggesting speed and precision. Most people never notice it, and once they do, they can't stop seeing it.

Negative space does quieter work everywhere. Generous margins make text feel calm and premium. Space around a button tells your eye where to look. Crowding everything together signals cheapness or panic, which is why luxury brands and well-designed apps often look almost empty. The lesson for any presentation or pitch deck: what you leave out shapes how people read what you keep.
cards.example: Find the FedEx logo online and spot the arrow between the E and the x. Then open your last slide deck, pick the most crowded slide, cut a third of the text and widen the margins. Compare which version you'd rather present.
cards.takeaway: Empty space isn't wasted; it directs the eye and signals quality.

cards.title: Red Lentil Dal with a Greek Yogurt Finish
cards.body:
Dal is one of the cheapest, fastest high-protein vegetarian meals there is, and red lentils need no soaking. In a pot, soften a diced onion in 1 tbsp oil, then add 3 cloves of garlic, 1 tbsp grated ginger, 1 tsp each of cumin, turmeric and garam masala, and a pinch of chili flakes. Stir for a minute until fragrant.

Add 1 cup (200 g) of rinsed red lentils, a 398 mL can of diced tomatoes and 3 cups of water or stock. Simmer 20 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils collapse into a thick stew. Stir in two big handfuls of spinach until wilted, then season with salt and lemon juice.

Serve in two bowls, each topped with a generous scoop of plain Greek yogurt and chopped cilantro.
cards.example: Makes 2 servings at roughly 40 g protein each: about 25 g from the lentils and around 15 g from 3/4 cup of Greek yogurt. Add rice or naan for carbs on a training day, and double the batch: it tastes even better the next day.
cards.takeaway: Red lentils plus Greek yogurt: a 40 g protein dinner in 30 minutes.

cards.title: Bids for connection: small moments, big stakes
cards.body:
Psychologist John Gottman spent decades observing couples, and one of his most useful ideas applies to every relationship: bids. A bid is any small attempt to connect, like "look at this", a question, a joke or a sigh. The other person can turn toward it by responding, turn away by ignoring it, or turn against it with irritation.

In Gottman's research on newlyweds, the couples still together years later had turned toward each other's bids far more often than the couples who split up. Grand gestures mattered less than thousands of tiny responses.

The same holds for friends, family and teammates. People feel valued when their small bids land, and quietly drift away when they don't. Turning toward rarely takes more than a few seconds: looking up, asking a follow-up question, or laughing at the joke.
cards.example: A roommate says, "Ugh, long day." Turning away: you keep scrolling. Turning toward: you put the phone down and ask what happened. This week, notice three bids from people close to you and turn toward each one.
cards.takeaway: Relationships are built in tiny moments of turning toward each other.

cards.title: The back-rank mate: give your king air
cards.body:
One of the most common ways club games end is the back-rank mate. Your king sits safely castled behind three unmoved pawns, which is good, until an enemy rook or queen lands on your first rank. The pawns that protected the king now trap it, and it's checkmate.

The defence is simple: make luft, the German word for air. At a quiet moment, push one pawn in front of your king, usually h3 for White or h6 for Black, giving the king an escape square. Alternatively, keep a rook or queen guarding your back rank.

The attacking side of the idea matters just as much. When your opponent's king has no luft, look for ways to overload or deflect the pieces guarding their back rank. Often a sacrifice that removes one defender ends the game on the spot.
cards.example: White has castled kingside with pawns on f2, g2 and h2, and the only rook guarding the first rank gets lured away. Black plays Re1+ and it's mate, because the king can't step forward. One earlier h3 would have given the king h2 to escape.
cards.takeaway: Unmoved pawns protect your king until they imprison it; make luft.

quiz.question: In 1975, how did Gordon Moore revise his prediction?
quiz.explanation: Moore's original 1965 observation was a doubling every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years.

quiz.question: What effort should most hill repeats be run at?
options: A strong, controlled effort around 5K race effort
An all-out sprint on every repeat
quiz.explanation: Hill repeats should be hard but controlled, so form holds up across every repeat.

quiz.question: What does negative space do in a good design?
options: Fills gaps when the designer runs out of content
Acts as a shape of its own and guides where the eye goes
quiz.explanation: Good designers treat empty space as an active element that creates focus, calm and hidden shapes like the FedEx arrow.

quiz.question: In the red lentil dal, where does most of the protein come from?
quiz.explanation: About 25 g per serving comes from the lentils and around 15 g from the Greek yogurt topping.

quiz.question: Review: A company has a $25B market cap, $3B of operating cash flow and $1B of capex. What is its FCF yield?
What is luft in chess?
options: An escape square for the king made by pushing a pawn in front of it
A rook on the seventh rank
A pawn sacrifice in the opening
quiz.explanation: Luft (German for air) is a pawn move like h3 that gives a castled king room to escape back-rank checks.
